sections.markdown:
## C — Starting the engine, moving off and stopping, hand positions and the three steering methods, and the steps for backing up safely
Knowledge domain: the basic vehicle handling a South Carolina learner needs before the road skills, covering engine start-up checks, pulling away and braking, where the hands go on the wheel, when to use push/pull, hand-over-hand or one-hand steering, and how to reverse safely.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Because vehicles differ, look in your owner's manual to learn how to start the one you are driving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
To start the engine, put your right foot on the brake pedal, confirm the gear selector is in park, then turn the key to the on position or push and release the start button. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
Once the engine runs, look over the gauges and any dashboard indicator lights that need attention, such as fuel, oil, ABS or air bag warnings. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
To pull away, move the gear selector to D for drive and make sure the path ahead of the vehicle is safe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
Before moving, also check the sides, the rear and your blind spots, looking over your shoulder for any traffic or obstacles. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
Give a signal and, if it is safe, move your foot to the accelerator and press it gently. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
Build speed slowly and evenly, pressing the pedal with the top of your foot while your heel rests on the floor. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A01
To stop, first check your mirrors for traffic behind you, then shift your foot from the accelerator to the brake pedal. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A02
Keep steady pressure on the brake pedal until the vehicle has stopped. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A02
You turn the steering wheel toward the direction you want the vehicle to go, whether you are moving forward or in reverse. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A02
Hold the outside of the steering wheel with both hands on opposite sides, using a grip that is firm but gentle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A02
Grip the wheel with your fingers rather than your palms, keep your thumbs up along its face, and never turn it while holding the inside of the rim. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A02
Picturing the wheel as a clock face, your left hand belongs in the 7 to 9 o'clock area and your right hand in the 3 to 5 o'clock area. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A02
Both hands stay on the wheel at all times except when one is needed for another driving task, such as shifting gears, switching on the wipers or giving hand signals. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A02
When you first learn to handle a car or truck, pick lightly traveled rural roads if you can. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A02
When you can steer accurately and keep making the small corrections steering always needs, you are ready to practice skills such as turning and parking. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A03
Hand-to-hand steering, usually called push/pull steering, is the method for turning the wheel in normal forward driving above 10 to 15 mph. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A03
For push/pull steering, your left hand holds the wheel between 7 and 8 o'clock and your right hand between 4 and 5 o'clock. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A03
In push/pull steering one hand pushes the wheel up while the other slides up, grips and pulls down, and the pushing hand slides back toward its starting point to make adjustments. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A03
To bring the vehicle back into your intended path after a push/pull turn, simply reverse the hand motions. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A03
Keeping the hands in the 7 to 9 and 3 to 5 o'clock areas tends to reduce muscle strain, which means less steering that causes weaving within a lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A03
Since the hands and arms never cross over the wheel in push/pull steering, a frontal crash in a vehicle with a driver's air bag is less likely to injure your face, hands and arms. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A04
Push/pull is the preferred steering method, and the 2 and 10 o'clock hand position is not recommended because it can be dangerous in vehicles with air bags. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A04
Hand-over-hand steering is for turning the wheel at low speeds, for example at an intersection or while parking. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A04
For hand-over-hand steering, start with your left hand between 8 and 9 o'clock and your right hand between 3 and 4 o'clock. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A04
In hand-over-hand steering you use the right top third of the wheel to turn right and the left top third to turn left, repeating as needed, then reverse the process to straighten out. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A04
One-hand steering is only for backing up or for a short reach to controls such as the wipers, flashers or lights. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A04
When you must reach for a control, keep your other hand at the normal operating position of 8 to 9 or 3 to 4 o'clock, depending on how the wheel is designed. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A05
A 12 o'clock hand position is recommended only when you back up to the left or right and must turn in your seat to see the path behind you. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A05
Check behind the vehicle before you get in, because children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A05
To back up, keep your foot on the brake, shift into reverse and take hold of the wheel at 12 o'clock with your left hand. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A05
Rest your right arm on the back of the passenger seat and look straight out through the rear window. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A05
Glance at your mirrors from time to time while backing, knowing they do not show the area right behind the vehicle, and check a rearview camera now and then if you have one. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A05
Accelerate gently and keep your speed low in reverse, because a vehicle is much harder to steer when backing. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A06
While backing, steer a little toward the side you want the rear of the vehicle to move. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A06
If you are turning while you back up, make quick checks to the front and both sides. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A06
Keep looking toward the rear until the vehicle comes to a complete stop. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

Misconceptions: the two and ten o'clock grip is not recommended in air bag vehicles; mirrors do not show the area right behind the vehicle, so you turn and look through the rear window when backing; the steering wheel turns the way you want to go even in reverse; one-hand steering is not for normal forward driving.
Mnemonics: push/pull for normal speeds, hand-over-hand for slow turns, one hand only for backing or a quick reach; for starting, think brake, park, key.
Glossary: gear selector means the lever that chooses park, drive or reverse; push/pull steering means hand-to-hand steering in which the hands never cross the wheel; hand-over-hand steering means crossing the hands over the top of the wheel for low-speed turns; blind spot means an area around the vehicle where your view is blocked.

corpus_stability.reason: The South Carolina Driver's Manual prints a single edition line (Revised 06/2024) on its front cover; its disclaimer says legislative and SCDMV policy changes may make some content out of date until the agency incorporates them, and a possibly newer unlinked upload exists on the issuer site (freshness debt in the run jams), so the corpus is treated as revised at most about once a year, bound to the registered snapshot.
